slot.what: The counts of the dead, each with who gives it. The strip below shows when the plague came back.
slot.alt: A chart in three panels, every bar dashed as a claim or an estimate. Deaths a day in Constantinople: 5,000, then 10,000 and more by Procopius, and 5,000 to 16,000 by John of Ephesus, at first among the poor. The dead in all by John of Ephesus: 230,000 counted before the counting stopped, and over 300,000 taken off the streets, beside a city of perhaps 400,000 to 500,000 people. The share of the city who died by modern estimates: about a fifth, 20 to 40 percent, a quarter to half, and half, while some scholars since 2019 argue the toll was overstated. Below, a time line of the plague's return from 541 until the last great outbreak in 746 to 748.

blocks.nav: When and where did the Plague of Justinian break out?
blocks.h: When and where did the Plague of Justinian break out?
paras: In Egypt in 541, at the port of Pelusium on the eastern edge of the Nile delta, and in Constantinople, the capital, in the middle of spring 542. "It started from the Aegyptians who dwell in Pelusium," wrote
, who was in Constantinople when it came. Sources of the time date its start at Pelusium to 541, the
notes.
In the capital it ran for four months, about three of them at its worst, by

. The emperor sent soldiers and money to bury the dead no one else could bury, and when the old tombs were full, new graves were dug all around the city. Justinian himself fell ill: "he too had a swelling of the groin",
writes.

blocks.nav: What caused the Plague of Justinian, and what were its symptoms?
blocks.h: What caused the Plague of Justinian, and what were its symptoms?
paras: Plague, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis: first a fever so mild that no one expected to die of it, then within a day or a few days a swelling in the groin, the armpit or beside the ears, as
describes it. Its DNA has been read from the teeth of people buried in the 6th century.

In 2013 scientists from Munich, Mainz and the German armed forces confirmed the bacterium in 6th-century graves at Aschheim near Munich, and in 2016 a complete genome was read from Altenerding nearby, the
records. In 2025

in a mass grave of the mid-6th to early 7th century beneath the old hippodrome of Jerash in Jordan, "the first site where a plague mass grave has been confirmed both archaeologically and genetically", the
said in 2026.
How it spread is still argued. Rats on grain ships from Egypt are the old answer, yet none of the routes a
tested, by rat fleas, through the air or both, fits everything the sources describe.

blocks.nav: How many died across the empire?
blocks.h: How many died across the empire?
paras: No one counted the empire's dead, and the estimates lie tens of millions apart. The figures often quoted, 15 to 100 million dead over two centuries of waves, appear in the
, and a
gives 25 to 100 million.

called such figures the "maximalist position" in 2019, when they set out to test them. Earlier estimates "are founded on a small subset of textual evidence", they found, and laws, coins, papyri, inscriptions and pollen show no clear sign of a collapse. Some places, such as Constantinople in the first outbreak, may still have suffered higher losses,
Others disagree. Peter Sarris criticises the method and the use of sources in Mordechai and Eisenberg's work, the
notes, and many scholars still follow the sources' picture of a catastrophe in essence, the
says.
A model test shows how hard the sources' numbers are to fit together. In 2020 Lauren White and Lee Mordechai

, assuming 500,000 people. With the values they expected, the bubonic models gave about 315,000 to 340,000 dead, more than even the highest estimates, but over a shorter time than Procopius describes.

blocks.nav: Did the Plague of Justinian come back?
blocks.h: Did the Plague of Justinian come back?
paras: Yes, in waves for two centuries. Justinian declared it over in 544, but it broke out again in 557, came back in 570 and then returned about every 15 to 25 years until after the middle of the 8th century, the last great outbreak in 746 to 748, the
sets out. Most of these waves are "thinly documented", the
adds.
caught it as a schoolboy in Antioch and survived. Later outbreaks took several of his children, his wife and many of his family, and on its fourth visit to the city he lost a daughter and her son.
By the middle of the 8th century, after the plague and other setbacks, perhaps 30,000 to 40,000 people lived in Constantinople,
writes, and he adds that "all these figures are contested".
From a few eyewitnesses, from inscriptions and papyri, and since 2013 from the bacterium's own DNA.
Procopius wrote up what he saw in close imitation of Thucydides' account of the plague of Athens, as the
and

Wikipedia articles note. John of Ephesus, a churchman who lived through it too, wrote a long account of it, which survives in a later Syriac chronicle. Scholars trust Procopius more than John, who also gives the death of 99.9 percent of the people, as
note.
A Greek epitaph of 542 records that Bishop Varus of Zora in Syria died of swellings of the loins and armpits, the
records. The

counted 505 papyri dated to single years from 520 to 570 and found "neither an observable reduction nor a marked increase" in their number. The DNA shows where the bacterium was, but not how many it killed, the study stresses.
What stays open is the total and the share of the capital that died.
